rv.q: On Sugarland tackles deeply serious subjects, but watching it is no grim duty; it explodes with originality, playfulness and passion.
No! We should have made a day of it.
“On Sugarland,” a beautifully produced play that struggles to follow through on its ambitions.
On Sugarland spins an enormous web of intertwined stories and themes: loss, grief, ostracism, betrayal, unrequited love.
Sugarland is a gripping portrait of three families struggling against powers beyond their control.
Alesha Harris’ On Sugarland is both demanding and rewarding, requiring patience and fortitude as the long play makes its way to its shocking conclusion.
Whitney White’s direction of his actors is masterful.
Harris has created such dynamic, vibrant women.
Exhuming that foundational trauma, holding it up for audiences to feel, understand, and mourn, takes a daring and determined imagination that goes beyond words.
On Sugarland stubbornly remains a collection of elements that often feel strangely arbitrary.
So much of On Sugarland does get out of hand, some of it for reasons germane to the script, but too often for reasons undercutting the script.
Harris, director Whitney White, and a truly exquisite cast of actors keep this consistently compelling 2 ½-hour play from boiling over into melodrama.

cn.t: Harris' ambitious, poetic epic about Black communities and war's toll earns praise for its bold vision and performances, though critics note it struggles to fully realize its sprawling metaphorical reach.
